title: Single-sided unbalanced addLiquidity into sUSDS/phUSD Balancer V3 pool is MEV-extractable; caller-supplied minBPT is the only defence and there is no fresh on-chain quote
description: pool(uint256 minBPT, uint256 minUSDC) calls IBalancerVault.addLiquidity with AddLiquidityKind.UNBALANCED, passing only sUSDS on one side (and 0 on the other). Balancer V3 mathematically prices a single-sided UNBALANCED add as if the joiner first swapped half of the deposit through the pool to balance it, charging a swap fee on the implied imbalance, and then performs a proportional add. This means the BPT returned is highly sensitive to the pool's current sUSDS/phUSD spot price (i.e., the same as a swap). The only protection in the contract is the caller-supplied `minBPT`. The contract exposes `getIdealBPT()` for off-chain quoting, but: (1) it is NOT called atomically inside `pool()`; (2) it is computed before the transaction is mined and is therefore stale against the actual pool state at execution; and (3) no expiry/deadline is enforced. An MEV searcher seeing the queued `pool()` transaction can sandwich it: front-run by swapping sUSDS->phUSD (pushing phUSD relative to sUSDS up), let `pool()` execute against the now-skewed pool (the unbalanced add is interpreted as more imbalance and the pooler pays a much higher implicit swap fee, receiving less BPT), then back-run by reversing the swap. The extracted value comes out of the dispatcher's BPT (which belongs to the protocol).
exploit_path:
Setup: BalancerPoolerV2 holds X sUSDS after a sequence of mints. The authorized pooler bot reads getIdealBPT() at block N, computes minBPT = expected * 99% and submits pool(minBPT, ...) at block N+1.

Attack steps:
1. MEV bot sees the pending pool(...) tx in the mempool with X sUSDS to add unbalanced.
2. MEV bot front-runs: swap phUSD -> sUSDS on the BPT pool (or any path connecting phUSD<->sUSDS into this pool), pushing the pool out of balance such that sUSDS becomes 'over-weight'. Because UNBALANCED add semantically subtracts a swap-fee-equivalent for the imbalance the joiner causes, depositing sUSDS into an already sUSDS-heavy pool is taxed more.
3. pool() executes against the skewed pool. The single-sided UNBALANCED add returns substantially fewer BPT than the off-chain quote predicted, but is still >= minBPT if the pooler did not set minBPT tight enough — and pool() succeeds.
4. MEV bot back-runs: reverses the swap (sUSDS -> phUSD), pocketing the price impact.

Who profits: MEV searcher. Loss is borne by the protocol (fewer BPT minted to the dispatcher than fair).

Magnitude: For Balancer V3 weighted/stable pools, single-sided UNBALANCED-add MEV typically extracts a meaningful fraction of the pool's swap-fee-adjusted price impact for the add size. On a $10M-depth sUSDS/phUSD pool, a $250k pool() execution can leak 0.05-0.2% (~$125-$500). On a thinner pool (<$2M depth) or larger pool() amount, the leak grows superlinearly (the implied swap-fee compounds with state-of-pool imbalance).

The attack requires no flash loan if the searcher already holds inventory in either token, and Balancer V3's stable/boosted-pool fees do not prevent profitability when the searcher's swap fee is paid back to the pool LPs (of which the searcher is now buying into via the joiner's BPT mint, indirectly).
mainnet_realism: Balancer V3 implements UNBALANCED adds via `computeAddLiquidityUnbalanced` (BasePoolMath.sol), which explicitly charges a swap fee on the imbalance amount and returns BPT net of that fee. This is exactly the mechanic an attacker exploits. The Aave-Boosted sUSDS/phUSD pool would, like any V3 pool, expose this code path. Single-sided LP MEV against Balancer V2/V3 weighted and composable-stable pools is well documented (e.g., academic and Flashbots case studies on Curve/Balancer single-sided joins). For sUSDS specifically the ERC4626 rate is mostly slow-moving (sky-savings), so day-to-day rate manipulation is not a defence — only pool spot deviation from the rate-provider price is. If the pool is a Balancer V3 boosted pool with rate providers for sUSDS, the implied swap-fee penalty is computed against the rate-adjusted price; the MEV path still works because the front-run swap moves the spot relative to the rate, and that delta is exactly what the joiner pays.
recommendation: Three layered mitigations: (a) replace AddLiquidityKind.UNBALANCED with PROPORTIONAL adds — source the second-side token (phUSD) via on-chain mint-or-swap in the same tx so the joiner is not exposed to the imbalance fee at all; (b) before calling addLiquidity, read the pool's current spot via Vault.getPoolTokens / pool-token rate-provider and revert if the spot deviates from the rate-provider price by more than a tight threshold (e.g., 25bps) — this gates execution to non-manipulated states; (c) move pool() execution to a private mempool / commit-reveal (e.g., Flashbots Protect, MEV-Share, SUAVE) so sandwich front-runs cannot be inserted at all. Also: add a `deadline` parameter to pool() to limit the staleness of caller-supplied `minBPT`. Note: a naive recommendation to call IBalancerRouter.queryAddLiquidityUnbalanced(...) inside the active unlockCallback is NOT viable because Balancer V3 router queries open their own unlock context and will revert against a held lock; the on-chain freshness must come from raw pool/vault state reads or a separate, pre-pool() query whose result is signed and time-bounded.
severity_rationale: Downgraded from initial High guess to Medium. The vulnerability is real value leakage to MEV searchers via sandwich attacks on a single-sided UNBALANCED Balancer V3 addLiquidity. However C4 High requires direct theft via realistic attack path without external assumptions; here the assets at risk are the protocol's own BPT yield (a value leak, not direct user-fund theft), and the function is permissioned via onlyAuthorizedPooler, meaning only the protocol's operator bot calls it. The operator can mitigate sandwich risk by submitting through a private mempool (Flashbots Protect, MEV-Share). The on-chain code does not enforce this, so the leakage is realistic if operator submits publicly, but the attack path requires the external assumption that the operator broadcasts to the public mempool. Per C4: 'Assets not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements' — this fits Medium. The protocol's BPT yield being eroded by MEV is a clear value leak with stated external requirement (public mempool submission).
poc_notes: Forked mainnet at block 25134513 (Balancer V3 Vault 0xbA1333..., Router 0xAE563E..., sUSDS/phUSD pool 0x642BB6...). Baseline BPT 528.9e18 vs sandwiched BPT 425.9e18 — 19.46% BPT haircut (~194.6 sUSDS-equivalent value lost). Attacker net sUSDS profit: 181.9e18 on 3000 sUSDS capital. No AMM mocking. Uses public RPC https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com (env MAINNET_RPC_URL overrideable).
rejection_reason: Finding mischaracterises the standard off-chain-supplied minBPT slippage-protection pattern as a vulnerability. The user-supplied minBPT is frozen before the tx is mined, which is precisely what makes it safer than an in-tx computed floor — an in-tx floor would track the sandwich-manipulated pool state and provide zero protection. Recommendation #2 (read pool spot and compare to rate-provider price) has the same defect: the attacker controls the spot inside the sandwich. After removing the bad recommendations, the finding reduces to 'operator picks loose minBPT AND broadcasts publicly' — an operational/configuration concern, not a code bug. The code already exposes the correct hooks (minBPT parameter + getIdealBPT off-chain quote).
